name: QR Refund Scam
description: Fraudsters convince victims they need to scan a QR code to receive a refund or cashback. In reality, you can only SEND money by scanning a QR — you never receive money this way.
red_flags: Someone asks you to scan a QR code to 'receive' a refund, cashback, or prize
The QR was sent over WhatsApp or Telegram by an unknown contact
The payee name on the QR says 'Flipkart', 'Amazon', or a bank, but the UPI ID is a personal account (e.g. random123@ybl)
Pre-filled amount on the QR ends in 999 (e.g. ₹9,999 or ₹49,999)
Caller creates urgency — 'scan in the next 2 minutes or your refund will expire'
what_to_do: Stop immediately — scanning a QR SENDS money, it never receives it
Block and report the number on WhatsApp
Report the UPI ID at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930
Alert your bank if you already scanned and paid
example: A 'Flipkart customer care agent' called saying your order refund of ₹4,999 is pending. They sent a QR code via WhatsApp and said 'scan to receive the refund'. The QR payee name said 'Flipkart Refund Desk' but the UPI ID was someone123@ybl — a personal account with no Flipkart connection.

name: OLX / Marketplace Buyer Scam
description: A fake buyer on OLX or Facebook Marketplace contacts you, agrees to your price, and sends a QR code or UPI request claiming it is a payment 'verification' or 'token amount'. Scanning or accepting sends money TO them.
red_flags: Buyer insists on paying via a QR code they send to you, rather than using OLX's built-in payment
They ask you to enter your UPI PIN to 'accept' their payment — entering PIN always SENDS money
Buyer claims to be in the Army, Navy, or a government job to build trust quickly
The amount offered is suspiciously higher than your asking price
They request your bank account number and OTP under the guise of payment verification
what_to_do: Only accept payments after physically meeting the buyer or via COD
Never enter your UPI PIN to receive money — PIN is only for sending
Reverse image search the buyer's profile picture
Report the account on OLX and to cybercrime.gov.in
example: You listed a second-hand laptop for ₹25,000 on OLX. A 'Colonel Sharma' offered ₹27,000 and sent a UPI collect request for ₹1 as 'verification'. Accepting it shared your UPI details; subsequent collect requests drained ₹15,000 before you noticed.

name: Fake Customer Support Scam
description: Fraudsters pose as bank, TRAI, Amazon, or Paytm customer care agents and convince victims to share OTPs, install screen-sharing apps, or authorise UPI collect requests to 'resolve' a fake account issue.
red_flags: Unsolicited call claiming your bank account, UPI, or SIM is about to be blocked
Caller asks for your OTP, card CVV, or UPI PIN over the phone — legitimate agents never do this
You are asked to install AnyDesk, TeamViewer, or QuickSupport for 'remote assistance'
The support phone number was found via a Google search — official numbers are on the back of your card or on the bank website
Caller gives you a fake employee ID number to sound official
what_to_do: Hang up immediately — call back using the number printed on your debit/credit card
Never share OTP, PIN, or CVV — your bank's real agents will never ask
Do not install any app suggested by an unsolicited caller
Report the number to the National Cyber Crime portal (cybercrime.gov.in)
example: A caller identified himself as 'SBI YONO support' and said your KYC had expired. He asked you to share a screen-sharing app link and then an OTP to 'verify your account'. Within minutes ₹80,000 was transferred from your account via UPI.

name: Advance Fee / Fake Job Offer Scam
description: Scammers post fake job listings on LinkedIn, Indeed, or WhatsApp groups, then ask hired candidates to pay a 'security deposit', 'training fee', or 'registration fee' via UPI before work begins. The job never materialises.
red_flags: Job offer received with no formal interview — instant 'selection' via WhatsApp or Telegram
High-paying work-from-home job that requires 'only 2 hours a day'
Request for advance payment: registration fee, ID card fee, training material fee, or security deposit
Company name is similar to a real company but the email domain is Gmail or Yahoo
After paying one fee, more fees are demanded before 'salary release'
what_to_do: Verify the company on LinkedIn and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) portal
Never pay money to get a job — legitimate employers pay YOU
Search the job description and company name + 'scam' on Google
Report fake jobs to cybercrime.gov.in and the job platform itself
example: A recruiter messaged on LinkedIn offering a ₹45,000/month data entry job. After a WhatsApp 'interview', you were asked to pay ₹2,500 for an ID card and ₹5,000 for training. Once paid, the recruiter stopped responding.

name: Fake Lottery / Prize Scam
description: Victims receive a call, SMS, or WhatsApp message saying they have won a lottery, lucky draw, or KBC prize and must pay 'GST', 'processing fees', or 'courier charges' via UPI to claim the winnings.
red_flags: You receive a prize notification for a lottery or contest you never entered
The prize is contingent on paying GST, customs duty, or a processing fee upfront
Caller claims to be from KBC (Kaun Banega Crorepati), RBI, or a government department
You are given a tight deadline: 'pay within 24 hours or prize is forfeited'
Prize money is always a round crore figure (₹25 lakh, ₹50 lakh)
what_to_do: Ignore and block — you cannot win a lottery you never entered
The RBI never contacts individuals about prize money; no government body does
Never pay 'taxes' or 'fees' to collect any prize — this is the scam itself
Report to cybercrime.gov.in or call the national helpline 1930
example: You get an SMS: 'Congratulations! You have won ₹25 lakh in the KBC Lucky Draw. Your number was selected from Jio records. Pay ₹8,500 GST via UPI to release your prize within 6 hours.' KBC never randomly selects numbers — this is a scam.

name: Fake E-commerce / Too Good To Be True Deal
description: Scammers build cloned or brand-new shopping websites offering luxury goods (iPhones, laptops, gold jewellery) at impossibly low prices. After payment via UPI, the product is never delivered or a worthless substitute arrives.
red_flags: Price is 70–90% below the market rate (e.g. iPhone 15 for ₹5,000)
The domain was registered very recently (less than 6 months old)
No physical address, GST number, or verifiable contact information on the site
Payment is only accepted via UPI direct transfer — no COD or card option
The website URL is a misspelling or imitation of a real brand (e.g. flipkart-deals.in, amaz0n-sale.co.in)
what_to_do: Check the website's domain age using a WHOIS tool — new domains are a major red flag
Search the site name + 'scam' or 'review' before buying
Only buy from established platforms with buyer protection (Flipkart, Amazon, Myntra)
If you already paid, file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in and contact your bank for a chargeback
example: A Facebook ad showed 'Brand New iPhone 15 Pro — Diwali Sale ₹4,999'. The site (apple-india-offer.com, registered 2 weeks ago) had no contact details and insisted on UPI payment. After paying, the number went unreachable.
